readingInstruction: Read Psalm 23. This is the best known of all the psalms. Read it slowly, as though for the first time, and hear Jesus say, “I am the good shepherd.”
settingTheScene: Psalm 23 is a psalm of David, who had been a shepherd. He knew what it was to guard sheep from lions and bears, to lead them to water, to count them at night. Here he uses that experience to describe the LORD’s care for him. The psalm moves from the pasture to the valley to the banquet table to the house of the LORD. It follows the good shepherd of John 10.
observation: “The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want” (v. 1).
“He makes me lie down in green pastures” (v. 2).
“He leads me in paths of righteousness for his name’s sake” (v. 3).
“Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me; your rod and your staff, they comfort me” (v. 4).
“You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies; you anoint my head with oil; my cup overflows” (v. 5).
“Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life, and I shall dwell in the house of the LORD forever” (v. 6).
interpretation:
“The LORD is my shepherd.” This is the foundation. The covenant name of God, Yahweh, is joined with a word of personal care. He is not just the shepherd of Israel in general; he is mine. “I shall not want” means that under his care nothing essential will be lacking.

The first scene is the pasture. A sheep will not lie down unless it is free from fear, from hunger, from friction in the flock, and from pests. The shepherd must provide all of this. “He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters.” He restores my soul, meaning he brings me back when I wander, and renews me. He leads me in paths of righteousness, not because I deserve it but “for his name’s sake.” His reputation is bound up with his flock.

The scene shifts to the valley. “Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death.” The path to the good pasture often goes through dark ravines. David does not say if, but “though.” And notice the change from “he” to “you” in the middle of the psalm. When the danger is greatest, David speaks directly to the shepherd: “for you are with me.” The rod fights off predators and the staff guides and rescues. They comfort him.

Then the picture changes to a banquet. The host prepares a table in the presence of enemies. They cannot touch him. He anoints his guest’s head with oil, and the cup overflows. The shepherd is also a host.

The psalm ends in hope: “Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life.” The word translated “follow” is a strong word, like pursuing. God’s goodness and steadfast love chase after us. And the destination is secure: “I shall dwell in the house of the LORD forever.”

Jesus said, “I am the good shepherd.” He is the one who leads, protects, and dies for the sheep. The 23rd Psalm is fulfilled in him.
connection: Genesis 48:15 and 49:24 call God the shepherd of his people. Ezekiel 34:11-16 promises that God himself will seek and shepherd his sheep. Isaiah 40:11 pictures God gathering lambs in his arms. John 10:11-16, Hebrews 13:20, and 1 Peter 5:4 identify Jesus as the shepherd. Revelation 7:15-17 says the Lamb will be their shepherd and wipe away every tear. Psalm 16:11 and 27:4 speak of dwelling in his presence.
application:
Read the psalm aloud, putting your own name in: “The LORD is my shepherd, and I shall not want.”

Identify your valley right now. Say verse 4 to the Shepherd.

Memorize the psalm if you have not already. It will be with you in dark times.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what you lack and what you want him to shepherd.
Tell him about your valley, and that you are with him there.
Thank him for goodness and mercy following you.
